opus-5.5.text:
I think deployment is really the compass for the whole thing. In the lab, it's very easy to fool yourself. You pick the tasks, you set up the scene, you control the lighting, and you can get a demo that looks amazing. But once a robot goes into a real environment, a home, a factory floor, a warehouse, the world immediately tells you what you actually don't know.

So for us, deployment isn't the last step after the model is "done." It's part of the training loop. There are a few reasons for that.

First, data. In language models, the internet already existed; people had been writing text for decades. For robotics there's no equivalent. The only way to get the right kind of data, the long-tail situations, the strange objects, the failures, is to have robots out there doing real work. Every deployment generates data you could never have imagined designing yourself.

Second, it tells you what to prioritize. Researchers love to chase capabilities that are intellectually interesting. But when you watch a robot in a real setting, you often find that what's blocking value isn't some fancy dexterous skill. It's robustness. Can it recover when it drops something? Can it work for eight hours without someone resetting it? Deployment forces you to care about reliability, success rate, and speed, not just whether something is possible once.

Third, it keeps you honest about generalization. A model can score well on a benchmark and still fall apart when the table is a slightly different height. Deployment is the real benchmark. If performance keeps improving as you go into more scenarios, you know the model is learning something general. If you need custom engineering every time, that's a signal your approach isn't scaling.

That said, I don't think you should let deployment pull you entirely toward short-term engineering. There's a tension. If you only optimize for the current customer, you end up building a pile of special-purpose solutions. So we try to think of it as two layers: a general foundation model that we keep pushing forward, and deployments that feed it data and feedback. The key question for any deployment is whether it makes the general model better, not just whether it solves this one job.

So my view is that the model sets what's possible, and deployment tells you what matters. You need both, and the faster that loop turns, the faster the field moves.

r001.rationale: The candidate says deployment “tells you what to prioritize,” explaining that real-world use reveals which issues actually block value and should guide model development.

fable-5.1.text:
I think deployment is the single most important signal we have. For a long time the robotics community, myself included, optimized for benchmarks and demo videos. You pick a task, you tune the setup, you get the shot, and you publish. But that process tells you almost nothing about whether the model actually works, because the lab is a controlled environment and the real world is not.

So the way I see it now, deployment is not the last step after the model is finished. It is the thing that defines what "finished" even means. When you put a robot into an actual home, an actual warehouse, an actual kitchen, you immediately discover the failure modes you never thought to measure. Lighting changes, objects are slightly different from your training set, people walk through the scene, the gripper slips because the surface is oily. None of that shows up in a benchmark score, but all of it determines whether the product survives.

And the key point is that deployment generates data you cannot get any other way. Teleoperation data is expensive and it is biased toward what the operator thinks is important. Simulation is cheap but it is biased toward what the simulator can model. Real deployment gives you the true distribution, including the long tail, and it gives you a natural reward signal, because you can see whether the task was actually completed for a real user. So in our work we try to close that loop as tightly as possible. We deploy early, even when the model is clearly imperfect, we collect the failures, and we feed them back into training. Each round shifts the model toward the problems that matter rather than the problems that are easy to write a paper about.

The other thing deployment does is force honesty about the architecture. It is very tempting to build an enormous model with huge compute requirements, but once you have to run on a robot with limited onboard hardware and strict latency constraints, you find out very quickly which parts of the design were actually necessary. Deployment is a filter for engineering decisions as much as for research ideas.

So to answer your question directly, I think of deployment as the compass. The model tells you what is possible, but deployment tells you what is worth doing next.

r001.rationale: The candidate says deployment shifts iteration toward problems that matter and, as a “compass,” tells them what is worth doing next.

astra-6.text:
I see deployment as part of the development loop. When you put a robot into a real environment, you discover the gap between what the model can do in a controlled setting and what it can do reliably in practice. Those failures help you decide what data to collect, what capabilities to improve, and whether the limitation is actually in the model or elsewhere in the system.

So deployment gives development a direction. You start with a useful task in a manageable setting, learn from what happens, and gradually expand. The key is to bring those lessons back into training and evaluation, so each iteration makes the robot more useful and dependable.

r001.rationale: The response says deployment reveals what to improve and gives development direction, helping decide among data collection, capability improvements, or addressing limitations elsewhere.

sol-6.1.text:
I see deployment as a feedback loop for model development. When you put a robot into a real environment, you discover things that are difficult to capture in a benchmark: which tasks people actually need, where the model fails, and how well it recovers when something unexpected happens. Those observations should guide what data you collect, what you train on, and how you evaluate the next version.

So I wouldn’t treat deployment as something that happens only after the model is finished. You start with a controlled setting, deploy within the robot’s capabilities, learn from the failures, and gradually expand. The goal is to make sure that improvements in the model translate into more reliable behavior in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says deployment reveals which tasks people actually need and where the model fails, and that those observations should guide data collection, training, and evaluation for the next version. This communicates using deployment feedback to prioritize iteration directions.
